chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khishab, from al-Yazid ibn Ishaq al-Sha'r, from al-Abbas ibn Yazid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said: 'These common people claim that polytheism is more hidden than the creeping of an ant on a black cloak in a dark night.' He said: 'The servant does not become a polytheist until he prays for other than God, or sacrifices for other than God, or supplicates to other than God, the Mighty and Exalted.'

key_terms.دُبِيبِ النَّمْلِ: The creeping of an ant (metaphor for subtlety)

ai.seo_question: What are the three conditions that define a person as a polytheist in Shia theology?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this hadith to establish a precise legal threshold for major polytheism (shirk al-akbar), countering the lay belief that it is as subtle as an ant crawling in the dark. The Imam defines it strictly through the performance of core acts of worship—prayer, sacrifice, or supplication—directed to entities other than Allah, thereby distinguishing it from minor shirk or mere belief.
